title: Galactic Twin NGC 6744
caption: The spiral galaxy NGC 6744, imaged by the Dark Energy Camera on the Blanco 4-meter Telescope
celestial: NGC 6744 · constellation Pavo · about 30 million light-years away (source figure)
credit: Dark Energy Survey/DOE/FNAL/DECam/CTIO/NOIRLab/NSF/AURA. Image processing: R. Colombari & M. Zamani (NSF NOIRLab)

recognition.text: NOIRLab Image of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: A luminous core sits at the centre of NGC 6744, surrounded by spiral arms that span 175,000 light-years. At the lower right, at the end of one arm, is its companion galaxy, NGC 6744A, a faint blob. On the left, a faint extended arm is visible, a feature rarely seen in most images.

Found in the constellation Pavo, NGC 6744 lies around 30 million light-years away. Its anatomy resembles that of our own Milky Way, only larger. Even its companion echoes ours, in a pairing similar to the one between the Milky Way and the Large Magellanic Cloud, its dwarf companion.
Nobody can step outside the Milky Way to photograph it. Galaxies like NGC 6744 give astronomers a stand-in, showing how our home might look to an observer far away.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (35.76 x 22.39 arcminutes) and distance (30 million light years), the frame spans roughly 312,000 × 195,000 light-years. Its light set out about 30 million years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: The Dark Energy Camera on the Blanco 4-meter Telescope observed NGC 6744 in visible light through g and r filters and a hydrogen-alpha filter. The colours assigned to each filter are not published.

explore: Few images of NGC 6744 have ever gone this deep. It was made with the Dark Energy Camera on Cerro Tololo Inter-American Observatory's Víctor M. Blanco 4-meter Telescope in Chile. The image belongs to the DESI Legacy Imaging Surveys, an effort to build the largest 3D map of the night sky.
